lines.text: Do you know how the internet crosses oceans? Not by satellite. Almost all of it travels through cables lying on the sea floor.
Hundreds of these cables, more than one point four million kilometers in total, carry over ninety nine percent of the data between continents.
In deep water, a cable is only about as thick as a garden hose. Inside, glass fibers thinner than a hair carry pulses of laser light.
Light fades over distance. So every few dozen kilometers, a repeater boosts it, powered by electricity sent down the cable itself.
Near the coast, where anchors and fishing nets are a danger, the cable gets steel armor and is buried under the seabed.
Breaks still happen. Most are caused by ship anchors and fishing gear. Not sharks.
Then a repair ship sails out, hooks the cable up from the bottom, splices it on deck, and lowers it back down.
So a file you send to another continent with Orbi Transfer probably rides along the ocean floor. And every file gets its own QR code and passcode.
